segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics news digest for October 16th, 2026.
Today we cover breakthroughs in mobile manipulation, touch-sensitive robotics, and AI-driven skill learning.
Tune in for the latest!
From Robotics & Automation News, ETH Zurich scientists turn WUJI robotic hand into self-propelled mobile manipulator.
This report details the demonstration of a WUJI robotic hand achieving self-propelled locomotion and manipulation without a separate mobility system.
The research involved training the hand to utilize its fingers for crawling, recovering from falls, and navigating its surroundings.

Reinforcement learning was employed to develop the locomotion by accounting for the unique characteristics of each finger, enabling the compact mobile manipulator to perform self-supported tasks such as pressing keyboard keys and pushing objects.
This work integrates locomotion and physical interaction capabilities into a single robotic hand structure.
This research suggests a novel pathway for developing highly mobile and interactive robotic systems in the future.
From Robotics & Automation News, Tesla patent reveals touch-sensitive skin for robot hands.
This story details a filed US patent for a touch-sensitive skin designed to mold around robot fingers and palms for detecting contact, force, and pressure.
The patent describes a manufacturing process where tactile sensors are printed onto flexible materials and then heat-formed into three-dimensional shapes.
The proposed sensor utilizes overlapping conductive regions on flexible substrate layers to register pressure changes through capacitive and piezoresistive methods.
This technology emphasizes manufacturability using established techniques like screen printing and thermoforming for scalable production.
This innovation aims to advance humanoid robots beyond basic grasping by enabling them to feel how firmly they are manipulating objects.
This development suggests a significant step toward more sophisticated tactile interaction for advanced robotic systems.
From Robotics & Automation News, Skild AI trains robots to learn physical skills through self-play.

This report details a self-play training method utilizing the S1 model to teach robots physical soccer skills through simulated competition, resulting in the robots developing complex behaviors like dribbling and tackling through competitive interaction rather than explicit instructions.
The methodology involved the robots playing against increasingly capable versions of themselves within a simulation environment, allowing skills to emerge organically from a single objective.

After 140 years of simulation, the resulting learned policy was successfully transferred to a physical humanoid robot, demonstrating a method to reduce reliance on human demonstrations for teaching robots complex physical abilities.
This development signals a shift toward autonomous skill acquisition in robotics research.
From TheSequence, "The Sequence Robotics - Issue #952: One Brain, Many Bodies: Inside Skild AI's Robotics Bet"
reports on Skild AI's research into transferring robotic intelligence across different hardware.
The core finding centers on developing a method for learning body understanding independent of specific physical machine specifications.
The research involved connecting motor adaptation, video-prompted task learning, and self-play to achieve this goal.

The methodology focuses on separating intelligence from the physical machine so that the model learns a generalized understanding of a body rather than requiring explicit prior engineering of every detail.
The team aims for the model to acquire body understanding through experience.
The ultimate assessment involves testing these capabilities against real-world demands for speed, reliability, and safety in deployment.
This work suggests a pathway toward more adaptable and universally applicable artificial intelligence systems in robotics.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Logging and Observability Guide Review Part 4 | Cloud Robotics WG Meeting 2026-10-19"
reports on the progress of the Logging and Observability guide review.
The next Cloud Robotics Working Group meeting is scheduled for Monday, October 19, 2026, at 4:00 PM UTC, where the primary focus will be continuing the editing of the first draft of the guide.
The group intends to complete the guide's edits during this session and subsequently submit it to guest speakers for review.
Information regarding the meeting access and notifications is available through the designated channels.
Attendees are invited to join to participate in the ongoing guide revision process.
This focused session addresses the refinement of essential documentation for robotics systems.
The completion of this guide will establish a standardized approach for system data management across the domain.
Future developments in cloud robotics will benefit from this established framework for logging and observability.
From Robotics & Automation News, Pudu expands beyond service robots into semi-humanoids and quadrupeds.
This report details the company's recent advancements in developing more complex robotic forms.
At the IFA 2026 event, Pudu Robotics showcased these developments, including the D7 semi-humanoid and the D5-W quadruped robot.
The D7 model demonstrates advanced manipulation capabilities across its arms, waist, and head, with a capacity to lift up to twenty kilograms.
Furthermore, the D5-W robot integrates both wheels and legs, enabling navigation over varied terrain and the autonomous ability to recover from falls.
This diversification of product offerings positions Pudu in competitive sectors of industrial robotics.
This development signals a broadening scope for robotic application within the technology sector.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Closing the Loop: How Automated Plants Turn Wastewater into Process Water".
This story details the four-step process utilized by automated plants to treat industrial effluent into reusable process water, resulting in reduced freshwater consumption and discharge volume.
The successful reuse process involves diagnosing the water, engineering the appropriate treatment, piloting the system, and finally deploying the full-scale system.
Automation systems instrument the water loop using probes to measure conductivity, pH, and ORP, with a programmable logic controller managing chemical dosing and water diversion.
Recovered water is subsequently applied to applications such as cooling tower makeup, washdown, or process feed, each requiring specific quality standards.
Implementing these systems applies the control discipline from production lines by measuring actual input and verifying performance prior to scaling up operations.
This advancement demonstrates the applicability of industrial control methodologies to complex environmental reclamation challenges.
From Humanoid.guide, Faraday Future launches $2,490 FF Nova humanoid for schools.
This report details the introduction of the FF Nova, a humanoid research and teaching platform intended for educational use.
The launch involved the release of only one hundred initial invitation-only units of the Nova.
This platform measures forty-nine point seven centimeters and possesses the capability to walk, turn, and recover from being knocked over.
It incorporates various sensors and supports the Robot Operating System 2, with an optional software package also available for use.
A smaller, twenty-nine nine Nova Mini is also available for younger users, featuring visual block programming capabilities.
This development is part of a larger restructuring within the robotics business involving a recent acquisition.
The introduction of these educational robotics tools signals continued investment in accessible humanoid technology for learning applications.
From Google / Google AI (Keyword Blog), "An intelligent new shopping cart"
details the rollout of a new shopping tool designed to simplify holiday purchasing.
This system allows users to consolidate products from various retailers into a single location, thereby eliminating the need for multiple browser tabs.
The Universal Cart is integrated across Search and the Gemini application in the United States.
It functions by actively tracking price fluctuations, identifying applicable promotional codes, and suggesting viable payment methods for the shopper.
Purchases can be finalized securely through Google Pay or by directly transferring items to the merchant's website.
This mechanism is intended to enhance shopper confidence and control during the online shopping process.
The introduction of such integrated AI shopping assistance signals a trend toward more seamless and controlled digital commerce experiences.
From Humanoid.guide, "PNDbotics Adam humanoid climbs 1 meter box, post claims".
This report details the demonstrated ability of the PNDbotics Adam humanoid to ascend a one-meter high box.
The process involved the robot analyzing the obstacle, planning necessary movements, and executing a coordinated action where one foot was placed onto the surface before shifting its weight.
This ascent necessitated the robot supporting and raising its body while maintaining equilibrium, a process centered on the transfer of weight across the entire body structure.
This demonstration showcases advanced robotic planning and dynamic balance control.
Further developments in bipedal locomotion and obstacle negotiation are expected within the field of artificial intelligence and robotics.
From Robohub, "Robot Talk Episode 166 – Evolving robot bodies and brains, with Rika Antonova"
details research into using artificial intelligence to develop complementary robot hardware and algorithms with Rika Antonova from the University of Cambridge.
Antonova's research focuses on co-design, automated algorithm discovery, and reinforcement learning within robotics.
The discussion explored the integration of AI principles into the design of robotic systems, emphasizing the development of synergistic hardware and software components.

The methodology involved leveraging advanced machine learning techniques to automate the discovery of optimal algorithms for robotic tasks, building upon expertise from institutions such as Carnegie Mellon University and Stanford.
This work centers on creating more intelligent and adaptable robotic systems through integrated design processes.
This research points toward further advancements in creating more autonomous and adaptable robotic platforms.
From Waymo Blog, "Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route"
reports on the launch of Waymo's fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, which will aim for first riders in 2028 through a phased, safety-first approach.
The rollout process involves mapping local street networks and testing with autonomous specialists to ensure adaptation to Toronto's specific driving conditions.
This expansion includes a partnership with Element Fleet Management to generate employment opportunities in fleet management, validation driving, and customer service.
Data indicates that the Waymo Driver has been associated with significantly fewer serious accidents compared to human drivers based on autonomous driving data.
The service is designed to integrate with Toronto's existing transportation ecosystem while emphasizing safety and accessibility.
This development signals continued progression in the deployment of autonomous transportation technologies within urban environments.
And that's all the circuits for today!
From the WUJI hand walking on its own, remember to keep those algorithms humming.
Until tomorrow, keep building and exploring!
Bye for now.
